ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in Fig. 1, there is a circular paper with point O as the center and AB as the diameter. Point C is on the circle $\odot$O. The circular paper is folded along the diameter CF, causing point B to fall on point D on $\odot$O (not coinciding with point A). After restoring the paper, connect CB, CD, AD. Assume CD intersects diameter AB at point E. As shown in Fig. 3, when $AD=DE$, if $BC=2$, what is the length of $AD$?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution:} Given that $AD=DE$, \\
it follows that $\angle DAE=\angle DEA$, \\
given that $\angle DEA=\angle BEC$ and $\angle DAE=\angle BCE$, \\
it follows that $\angle BEC=\angle BCE$, \\
considering the circle paper folded along the line CF, \\
it follows that $\angle ECO=\angle BCO$, \\
furthermore, given that $OB=OC$, \\
it follows that $\angle OCB=\angle B$, \\
given that $\angle ECO=\angle B$, and $\angle CEO=\angle CEB$, \\
it follows that $\triangle CEO\sim \triangle BEC$, \\
resulting in $\frac{CE}{ED} = \frac{BE}{CE}$, \\
and therefore $CE^2=EO\cdot BE$, \\
let EO=x, EC=OC=OB=a, \\
hence $a^2=x(x+a)$, \\
solving yields, x= $\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}a$ (negative value discarded), \\
therefore, $OE= \frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}a$, \\
therefore, $AE=OA-OE=a- \frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}a= \frac{3-\sqrt{5}}{2}a$, \\
given that $\angle AED=\angle BEC$, $\angle DAE=\angle BCE$, \\
it follows that $\triangle BCE\sim \triangle DAE$, \\
resulting in $\frac{BC}{AD} = \frac{EC}{AE}$, \\
given that $BC=2$, \\
$\frac{2}{AD} = \frac{a}{\frac{3-\sqrt{5}}{2}a}$, \\
thus, $AD=\boxed{3- \sqrt{5}}$.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: From the attached figure, it can be seen that there are three circular paper-piece schematic diagrams, Figure 1, Figure 2, and Figure 3. In each figure, AB is a horizontal diameter, and O is on AB and is the circle center; C, D, and F are all marked on the circumference, and CF is an oblique diameter passing through O. In Figure 3, CB, CD, and AD are connected, line CD intersects diameter AB at E, and E is located between A and O; D is on the upper-left circumference, C is on the lower circumference, and B is on the right-end circumference. Reasoning: It is known that AD=DE, so △ADE is an isosceles triangle, hence ∠DAE=∠AED. Because E is on AB and C, D, E are collinear, ∠AED and ∠BEC are vertical angles, ∠AED=∠BEC. Also because ∠DAE=∠DAB, and ∠DAB and ∠DCB subtend the same arc DB, so ∠DAB=∠DCB; since C, D, E are collinear, ∠DCB=∠BCE. Therefore ∠DAE=∠BCE. Thus ∠BEC=∠BCE, so △BCE is an isosceles triangle, BE=BC. The folding is performed along diameter CF, B is folded to D, and C and O are on the crease CF, so the crease bisects ∠BCD, that is ∠BCO=∠OCD, namely ∠BCO=∠ECO. Also OB=OC, so △OBC is an isosceles triangle, ∠CBO=∠BCO. Since B, E, O are collinear, ∠CBE=∠CBO, so ∠CBE=∠ECO. And EO and EB are collinear and in the same direction, so ∠CEO=∠CEB. Thus △CEO∼△BEC. From the similarity relation, C↔B, E↔E, O↔C, so CO corresponds to BC, and CE corresponds to BE. Also BE=BC was obtained earlier, therefore from CO/BC=CE/BE, CO=CE can be obtained. Let CE=CO=OB=a, OE=x. From similarity it can also be obtained that OE/CE=CE/BE, that is CE²=OE·BE. In the figure, E is on the left side between O and B, so BE=BO+OE=a+x, hence a²=x(a+x). Let t=x/a, then 1=t(1+t), solving gives t=(√5−1)/2, that is OE=((√5−1)/2)a. Therefore AE=AO−OE=a−((√5−1)/2)a=((3−√5)/2)a. Next look at △BCE and △DAE: already ∠BEC=∠AED, and ∠BCE=∠DAE, so △BCE∼△DAE. Corresponding sides give BC/AD=CE/AE. Substituting CE=a, AE=((3−√5)/2)a, BC=2, gives 2/AD=a/(((3−√5)/2)a)=2/(3−√5). Therefore AD=3−√5.
